Question: Do you expect free refills (at least of the sandwiches and possibly also scones) as standard as part of afternoon tea (i.e. the traditional British meal often served in hotels)?
Answer: No. As a concept, it sounds very American, when afternoon tea is archetypally British. Encouraging sheer greed sounds horribly distasteful, and it would surely encourage the establishment to concentrate on cheapness at the expense of quality. In any case, I can't think of a single time when I've gone out for afternoon tea and the meal was anything but generous. After all, it will typically involve delicious sandwiches, fresh scones, with cream and jam, and good cake too, as well as a pot of tea - it's not going to be exactly light on either calories or carbohydrates. And you'll probably still be expecting to have dinner later, too. I enjoy good food, as the bathroom scales regrettably confirm. But I can't conceive of needing free refills in such a meal. Tacky and revolting as an idea!

Question: Do I need GCSE lang paper 2 as well as P1 to get a grade 4? Or can I pass with just completing paper 1?
Answer: Almost certainly you will need to do both papers. I suppose that it might, theoretically, be just about possible to scrape a grade 4 if you got practically full marks on just Paper 1, but you can't depend on that, and there may well be rules saying that you have to take both papers; I don't know. If you are so brilliant that you could get away with doing one paper on its own, you should have no problem with taking both of them. And of course you could also be slightly less wonderful than you think, and find you've miscalculated. Take them both!

Question: Is 5 considered a B in IGCSE?
Answer: No, it isn't. 4 and 5 are lower and higher parts of a C. You'd need a 6 for it to be considered equivalent to a B.

Question: Did your parents ever say you were an accident? How did you respond?
Answer: No, and neither did we ever say anything of the kind to any of our children, if you discount the minor accident of planning for a second baby, but unexpectedly having a third one delivered five minutes later. These things happen, and we're mostly over the shock now (forty years later)… But my youngest aunt, born nine years after the youngest of her three elder siblings, did once say this bitterly and accusingly to Grandma. “You never wanted me! I was just a mistake!” Grandma apparently took the accusation very calmly. “If it comes to that, dear,” she said, “you were all mistakes!” Aunty was born in 1924, the baby of the family, and the other three were born in 1910, 1912 and 1915. Despite what you sometimes hear, many parents in those days were fairly good at avoiding too many unwanted pregnancies.
